content: Aluminum chloride is a chemical compound that has received FDA approval for use in controlling minor hemorrhage during dental restorative procedures. It is important to note that hypersensitivity reactions are a common adverse effect associated with its use. For adult patients, aluminum chloride is indicated for the control of minor bleeding during dental procedures. To use, a small amount of Hemoban should be dispensed into a clean dappen dish or disposable cup. For hemorrhage control prior to making a restorative impression, a retraction cord should be soaked in aluminum chloride and then placed into the gingival sulcus using a cord-packing instrument. Aluminum chloride is compatible with all impression techniques, but it is recommended to gently rinse critical areas with water before applying addition-type (VPS) impression materials to avoid interference with the setting reaction of the impression material. In other situations requiring minor hemorrhage control, a cotton pellet soaked in aluminum chloride can be applied to the area for several seconds, followed by gentle rinsing with water. There is limited information available regarding off-label uses of aluminum chloride in adult patients, whether guideline-supported or not. For pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding both FDA-labeled and off-label uses of aluminum chloride. Aluminum chloride should not be used in individuals with known sensitivities to the compound. It is intended for professional dental use only and should not be swallowed. It must be kept out of reach of children. Adverse reactions to aluminum chloride are not well-documented in clinical trials or postmarketing data. Similarly, there is limited information on drug interactions involving aluminum chloride. Regarding use in specific populations, there is no FDA guidance on the use of aluminum chloride during pregnancy, labor and delivery, or in nursing mothers. Additionally, there is no FDA guidance on its use in pediatric, geriatric, gender-specific, or racial populations, nor in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. There is also no guidance on its use in immunocompromised patients or in women of reproductive potential and men. Aluminum chloride is administered topically. However, there is limited information on monitoring requirements for its use. There is also no information available on its IV compatibility or chronic overdose. Pharmacologically, aluminum chloride is formulated to control minor hemorrhage during dental restorative procedures. It is commonly used with retraction cords or cotton pellets and contains 25% aluminum chloride. There is limited information on its structure, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology. Clinical studies on aluminum chloride are limited, and there is no detailed information on how it is supplied. It should be stored at temperatures between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C) and protected from freezing. There is limited information available regarding patient counseling for aluminum chloride. Additionally, the interaction between alcohol and aluminum chloride has not been established, so patients should consult their doctor about the effects of consuming alcohol while using this medication.
